newsitem.title: USA: Candidates spar over campaign debates.
newsitem.headline: Candidates spar over campaign debates.

text.p: Republican Jack Kemp called Ross Perot's Reform Party unnecessary and Democrat Al Gore blamed Bob Dole for excluding the Texas billionaire and his running mate from debates, according to excerpts from television interviews released on Friday.
But the No. 2 man on Perot's ticket, economist Pat Choate, took aim instead at the major television networks for refusing to sell large blocks of time to the Reform Party organisation.
One unnamed network, he said on the PBS programme "Talking with David Frost," offered Perot "75 seconds to make our case" between now and election day Nov. 5.
"They're no longer independent, they're owned by industrial and other corporations who have interests before the federal government," Choate said of the networks.
Each of the three vice-presidential candidates was interviewed separately by Frost this week and excerpts were released in advance of the program's airing Friday.
Kemp denied the decision to bar Perot from the debates next month was unfair, saying members of the bipartisan commission that organises the sessions voted unanimously against his inclusion.
"I don't think there's any need for a Reform Party," Kemp said. "Not to be disrespectful to Ross Perot, who I admire in many ways as an entrepreneur and a patriot, but ... we don't need it.
Gore said he and President Clinton favoured Perot's inclusion but that Dole then would have refused to take part.
"As a matter of principle, he should have been in ... but Senator Dole made it clear that he would not debate at all unless Ross Perot were excluded," Gore said.

Negotiators for the Republican and Democratic parties agreed last weekend to hold two presidential and one vice presidential debate. Dole and Clinton were scheduled to debate Oct. 6 in Hartford, Connecticut and Oct. 16 in San Diego.
The vice presidential encounter was set for Oct. 9 in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Lawyers for Perot have filed suit in federal court to force his inclusion and also have requested that the Federal Communications Commission investigate the Reform Party's complaint that networks had refused to sell him enough air time for his campaign.

In a letter to the FCC, the lawyers alleged that ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox had "consistently refused to sell adequate air time to Mr. Perot." Perot has relied on infomercials to get his views across to voters.
They called on the FCC to ensure Perot was given the opportunity to present his views under rules that mandate equal access by a political candidate.
The FCC Thursday asked attorneys for the networks for a "response, if any, to the pertinent portions of the complaint."
